results.title: Pollack–Pomerance sieve bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an absolute constant $C > 0$ such that for every set $P$ of primes and every real $x > 1$, the number of integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le x$ that are divisible by no prime in $P$ is at most $C x \exp(-A_P(x))$, where $A_P(x) = \sum_{p \in P,\ p \le x} 1/p$.

results.title: Integers whose sum of divisors is not divisible by $p$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an absolute constant $C > 0$ such that for every prime $p$ and every real $x \ge e^p$, the number of integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le x$ for which $p$ does not divide the sum of divisors $\sigma(n)$ is at most $C x (\log \log x / \log x)^{1/(p-1)}$.

results.title: Generating function of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G(t)$ be the inverse, in the ring $\mathbb{Q}[[t]]$ of formal power series, of the series $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^n}{n + 1} t^n$, which is invertible because its constant coefficient is $1$.

results.title: Bernoulli numbers of the second kind
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the Bernoulli number of the second kind $B_n^*$ is the rational number $n!$ times the coefficient of $t^n$ in $G(t) \in \mathbb{Q}[[t]]$, the inverse of the formal power series $\sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^k}{k + 1} t^k$. Thus $G(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} B_n^* t^n / n!$.

results.title: Generating function of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind as an inverse
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The generating function $G(t)$ of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind equals the inverse, in the ring $\mathbb{Q}[[t]]$ of formal power series, of the series $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^n}{n + 1} t^n$.

results.title: Bernoulli numbers of the second kind as scaled coefficients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, the Bernoulli number of the second kind $B_n^*$ equals $n!$ times the coefficient of $t^n$ in the generating function $G(t) \in \mathbb{Q}[[t]]$ of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind.

results.title: Defining identity of the generating function of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Defining identity of the generating function of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind. In the ring $\mathbb{Q}[[t]]$ of formal power series, the generating function $G(t)$ of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind satisfies $G(t) \cdot \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{(-1)^n}{n + 1} t^n = 1$.

results.title: Coefficient identity for the generating function of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Coefficient identity for the generating function of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind. Let $g_i$ be the coefficient of $t^i$ in the generating function $G(t) \in \mathbb{Q}[[t]]$ of the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind. For every natural number $n$, the sum of $g_i \cdot (-1)^j / (j + 1)$ over all pairs $(i, j)$ of natural numbers with $i + j = n$ equals $1$ if $n = 0$ and $0$ if $n \ge 1$.

results.title: Recurrence for the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n \ge 1$, the Bernoulli numbers of the second kind $B_k^*$ satisfy $B_n^* / n! = -\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (B_k^* / k!) \cdot (-1)^{n-k} / (n - k + 1)$.

results.title: Integer polynomial map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $m$, an integer polynomial map from $n$ variables to $m$ components is an $m$-tuple $F = (F_0, \dots, F_{m-1})$ of polynomials with integer coefficients in the $n$ variables $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$.

results.title: Evaluation of an integer polynomial map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F = (F_0, \dots, F_{m-1})$ be an integer polynomial map from $n$ variables to $m$ components. The value of $F$ at a point $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ is the point $(F_0(x), \dots, F_{m-1}(x)) \in \mathbb{Z}^m$.

results.title: Reduction of an integer polynomial map modulo a natural number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F = (F_0, \dots, F_{m-1})$ be an integer polynomial map from $n$ variables to $m$ components and let $p$ be a natural number. For $x \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^n$, the value of the reduction of $F$ modulo $p$ at $x$ is $(\bar F_0(x), \dots, \bar F_{m-1}(x)) \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^m$, where $\bar F_i$ is the polynomial obtained from $F_i$ by reducing its coefficients modulo $p$.

results.title: Iterates of an integer polynomial map
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ be an integer polynomial map from $n$ variables to $n$ components, viewed as the map $\mathbb{Z}^n \to \mathbb{Z}^n$ given by evaluation. For a natural number $k$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}^n$, the $k$-th iterate of $F$ at $x$ is $F^k(x)$, the result of applying $F$ to $x$ exactly $k$ times; in particular $F^0(x) = x$.

results.summary: The law of the generation size `Z_n` of the Galton–Watson process with offspring law `ν` started from one individual: `Z_0 = 1` and, given `Z_n = z`, `Z_{n+1}` has law `ν^{∗z}` (`Measure.convPow ν z`).

results.title: Mean offspring number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The mean offspring number `m = E ξ = ∑ k ν{k} ∈ [0, ∞]`.

results.title: Extinction probability of a Galton–Watson process
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The extinction probability `q = sup_n P(Z_n = 0)`, the limit of the probabilities of extinction by generation `n` (`tendsto_law_real_zero`). On a path space carrying the process the events `{Z_n = 0}` increase with `n` (`0` is absorbing), so `q` is the probability of eventual extinction; this file describes the process through its generation laws and does not construct the path space.

results.title: Iterates of the offspring generating function stay in (0, 1)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The iterates `f^[n](s)` of the offspring generating function stay in `[0, 1]` for `s ∈ [0, 1]`.

results.title: Iterates of the generating function at zero are nondecreasing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The iterates `f^[n](0)` of the offspring generating function are non-decreasing.

results.title: Limit of generating-function iterates is the least fixed point
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `sup_n f^[n](0)` is the least fixed point of `f` in `[0, 1]` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).

results.title: Least fixed point equals one iff mean offspring is at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The least fixed point is `1` iff the mean offspring number is at most `1`, provided the offspring number is not almost surely `1` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).

results.title: Generating function of the n-th generation size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The generating function of `Z_n` is the `n`-th iterate of the offspring generating function on `[0, 1]` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).

results.title: Mean generation size of a Galton–Watson process
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The mean generation size is `E Z_n = m ^ n` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).

results.title: Extinction by generation n is nondecreasing in n
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `P(Z_n = 0)` is non-decreasing in `n`.

results.title: Extinction by generation n converges to the extinction probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `P(Z_n = 0)` converges to the extinction probability.

results.title: Extinction probability is the least fixed point
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The extinction probability is the least fixed point of the offspring generating function in `[0, 1]` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).

results.title: Galton–Watson extinction criterion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Extinction is certain iff the mean offspring number is at most `1`, provided the offspring number is not almost surely `1` (Athreya–Ney 1972, ch. I).

results.title: Exponential generating function of the binomial transform
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ and $(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be real sequences with $b_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} a_k$ for every $n$, and let $A : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be any function. For every real number $t$, if the series $\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n t^n / n!$ converges absolutely with sum $A(t)$, then the series $\sum_{n \ge 0} b_n t^n / n!$ converges absolutely with sum $e^t A(t)$.

results.title: Binomial transform
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The binomial transform of an integer sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ is the falling k-binomial transform of $a$ with $k = 1$, the sequence whose $n$-th term is $\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} 1^{n-i} a_i$.

results.title: Binomial transform as a binomial sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every integer sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n$-th term of the binomial transform of $a$ equals $\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} a_i$.

results.title: Multiple binomial transform
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The binomial transform sends an integer sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ to the sequence $(b_n)_{n \ge 0}$ given by $b_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} a_i$. For a natural number $r$, the $r$-fold binomial transform of $a$ is obtained by applying the binomial transform $r$ times in succession; the $0$-fold transform of $a$ is $a$ itself.

results.title: The k-fold binomial transform is the falling k-binomial transform
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every integer sequence $a$ and every integer $k$: if $k \ge 0$, applying the binomial transform $k$ times to $a$ gives the falling $k$-binomial transform of $a$; if $k < 0$, applying the inverse binomial transform (the falling $(-1)$-binomial transform) $-k$ times to $a$ gives the falling $k$-binomial transform of $a$. In both cases the equality is one of integer sequences.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field and let $a : \mathbb{N} \to K$ be a sequence with ordinary generating function $A(X) = \sum_n a_n X^n \in K[[X]]$. results.title: Cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A cell of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a pair $(r, c)$ of a row $r \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and a column $c \in \{0, \dots, n-1\}$.

results.title: Adjacent cells
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two cells $x$ and $y$ of the $3 \times n$ rectangle are adjacent when they share an edge: they lie in the same row and their columns differ by $1$, or they lie in the same column and their rows differ by $1$.

results.title: Square and domino tiles
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $d$ of cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a square-or-domino tile when it consists of exactly one cell, or of exactly two cells that are adjacent.

results.title: Characterization of square and domino tiles
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A set $d$ of cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a square-or-domino tile if and only if either $d = \{x\}$ for some cell $x$, or $d = \{x, y\}$ for some distinct adjacent cells $x$ and $y$.

results.title: Square-and-domino tilings
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A square-and-domino tiling of the $3 \times n$ rectangle is a finite family $T$ of sets of cells such that every member of $T$ is a square-or-domino tile (a single cell or two adjacent cells), any two distinct members of $T$ are disjoint, and every cell of the rectangle lies in some member of $T$.

results.title: Vertical-fault-free families
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A family $T$ of sets of cells of the $3 \times n$ rectangle, with columns numbered $0, \dots, n-1$, is vertical-fault-free when for every natural number $k$ with $k + 1 < n$ some member of $T$ contains two cells of the same row lying in columns $k$ and $k + 1$. For a square-and-domino tiling this says that every internal vertical boundary is crossed by a horizontal domino.

results.title: Number of vertical-fault-free tilings of the $3 \times n$ rectangle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, this is the number of square-and-domino tilings of the $3 \times n$ rectangle that are vertical-fault-free.

results.title: Recurrence for vertical-fault-free tilings of the $3 \times n$ rectangle
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For $n \ge 1$, let $V_n$ be the number of vertical-fault-free tilings of the $3 \times n$ rectangle by unit squares and dominoes. Then $V_1 = 3$, $V_2 = 13$, $V_3 = 26$, $V_4 = 66$, $V_5 = 154$, $V_6 = 380$, and $V_n = V_{n-1} + 4 V_{n-2} - V_{n-3} - V_{n-4}$ for every $n \ge 7$.
